name: Silicone/Gore-Tex nasal implant
lead: Silicone and expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE, sold as Gore-Tex) nasal implants are synthetic (alloplastic) materials placed in the nose, most often to raise a low nasal bridge. A carved implant sits along the dorsum and adds height and a straighter profile line, and a separate piece can be used to project the tip. They are an alternative to the patient's own cartilage and are particularly associated in the literature with augmentation rhinoplasty in Asian patients. [1][2]

Reviews describe a long history of alloplastic implant use in Asia, while noting that some patients are unsuitable for or decline synthetic materials and that costal (rib) cartilage is an alternative. [1] In looksmaxxing forums, nose-job outcomes in Asian patients are a recurring topic, as is the broader choice between silicone and other implant materials for facial work. [9][13]
infobox: Autologous rib, septal or ear cartilage [5][7]

paras: Reviews note that typical Asian noses often have a low dorsum, weak lower lateral cartilages, columellar retraction and thick sebaceous skin, so patients usually seek augmentation rather than reduction.[2][3] One review describes the choice of dorsal implant material as depending partly on skin thickness, and notes that autologous cartilage has the lowest infection risk among graft materials but carries a significant revision risk linked to complications including warping.[4]

Silicone, a family of siloxane polymers named by F. S. Kipping in 1901, is described on Wikipedia as having high biocompatibility and low toxicity, and its gel and solid forms appear in breast, pectoral and testicular implants as well as dressings. [12] Solid carved silicone is the traditional dorsal implant in much of East Asia. [1]

ePTFE descends from PTFE, discovered accidentally by Roy Plunkett at DuPont in 1938. [11] Bob Gore created the expanded form by stretching heated PTFE rods, and the porous result is about 70 percent air; W. L. Gore and Associates uses it in vascular grafts, sutures, heart patches and facial plastic surgery implants including nasal augmentation. [10][11] Wikipedia notes ePTFE is nearly inert and that its porosity allows body tissue to grow into it. [10]

A 2019 review states that costal cartilage is abundant and highly biocompatible but difficult to use and associated with a high complication rate, prompting techniques designed to reduce its drawbacks.[5] A retrospective series of 83 patients reviewed graft-related and harvest complications and satisfaction after autologous costal cartilage rhinoseptoplasty.[6] Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article says synthetic implants are used only when autologous options are unavailable, and that autologous grafts carry less risk of rejection.[7]

The tradeoffs described are donor-site surgery and graft warping or resorption with cartilage, versus implant-related risks with synthetic material, and the preferences of the individual patient and surgeon. [1][4][5]

Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article reports that revision surgery is needed in roughly 5 to 15 percent of rhinoplasties of all kinds and lists bleeding, infection, adhesions and septal perforation among risks. [7] It states that autologous cartilage and bone grafts are preferred over artificial implants because of lower rejection and complication rates. [7]

A review in Facial Plastic Surgery notes that the choice of dorsal material depends partly on skin thickness and that autologous cartilage carries a significant revision rate linked to warping. [4] Costal cartilage is described as highly biocompatible but difficult to use, with a high complication rate. [5] Surgeons in these reviews describe case-by-case choices between implant and graft.

Evidence is in the form of narrative reviews and retrospective series, such as the 83-patient costal cartilage series.[6] Registered trials of implants in the nose (for example Latera) concern nasal valve collapse rather than cosmetic bridge augmentation.[8]

timeline.event: F. S. Kipping coins the term 'silicone'. [12]
Roy Plunkett discovers PTFE at DuPont. [11]
Bob Gore and Wilbert Gore develop expanded PTFE (Gore-Tex). [10]
A US appeals court rules Gore is the legal inventor of ePTFE. [10]
Facial Plastic Surgery Clinics review describes alloplastic implants' long history of safety in Asia. [1]
Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery publishes an 83-patient series on autologous costal cartilage in Asian rhinoplasty. [6]
Review of rib cartilage trends in Asian rhinoplasty is published. [5]

lore.intro: Community posts about Asian rhinoplasty focus on how natural the result appears rather than on implant material specifically.[9]

claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks why many Asian rhinoplasty results look artificial or doll-like and how to keep a natural look while refining details.[9]
claims.experts: Reviews say aesthetic goals should be tailored to the patient's ethnicity and culture, and that preoperative analysis and anatomy differ from Caucasian rhinoplasty.[3]

claims.claim: Silicone is a good implant material
claims.believers: Looksmax.org members weigh silicone against titanium, PEEK and Medpor for facial implants, noting its lower price and that screw fixation can stabilise it; this thread concerns facial implants in general. [13]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes silicone as highly biocompatible and widely used in implants, while rhinoplasty reviews say autologous grafts have lower rejection and complication rates. [7][12]

card.summary: Synthetic bridge implants for low noses, long used in Asian rhinoplasty, with cartilage as the main alternative.
card.note: Evidence here is reviews and case series; patients may not be suitable for or accept synthetic materials.

quick.overview:
Silicone and Gore-Tex implants are synthetic materials placed in the nose to raise a low bridge. Reviews describe a long history of alloplastic implant use in Asia.

The alternative is the patient's own cartilage, such as rib, which has its own complication profile.
quick.mechanism: A carved implant is placed along the nasal dorsum to increase height.
quick.risks: Reviews say some patients are unsuitable for or decline alloplastic materials; Wikipedia says autologous grafts carry less rejection risk. Specific complication rates for silicone and Gore-Tex were not reviewed here.

chain: A carved silicone or ePTFE implant is placed along the nasal bridge
Dorsal height rises and the profile line straightens
A more defined nose that balances the forehead-to-chin profile
angle.text: For low-bridge noses, adding material is the direct route to a higher dorsum, which reviews describe as the usual aim in Asian rhinoplasty. Implants avoid a cartilage donor site, while autologous cartilage avoids a foreign material.
